newsitem.title: HAITI: Haitians to vote amid frustration, uncertainty.
newsitem.headline: Haitians to vote amid frustration, uncertainty.

text.p: Haitians showed uncertainty, frustration and apathy ahead of Sunday's elections, the latest step in an international effort to bring democracy and development to the severely afflicted country.

Discontent simmered against the 14-month-old government of President Rene Preval as life got harder, not better, for many Haitians. Violence had surged, but the U.N. peacekeeping force planned to bid farewell to the Caribbean nation in the summer.
The ruling Lavalas Political Organisation had a split with Preval's one-time ally, former President Jean-Bertrand Aristide, leading criticism against him behind the scenes.

Prime Minister Rosny Smarth last week survived a no-confidence motion which said the government was "incapable of coping with the current social, economic and political disorder and preventing the country from plunging into an ungovernable state."

Although diplomats and U.N. officials dismissed the chances of a violent return by forces loyal to the succession of dictators and generals who traditionally ruled the poorest country in the Western Hemisphere, Haiti still had a long way to go, they said.

"There is a generalized perception that the government hasn't been active enough," U.N. special representative Enrique Ter Horst told Reuters. "You have an economy that is dead in the water. There is uncertainty and frustration."

Sunday's elections will be for Senate seats and local councils. Officials and analysts expected a low turnout for these elections. Their significance lay in bringing local democracy to Haiti for the first time.
The councils also will appoint judges, an important task in a country where the judiciary barely functions.
"These elections are enormously important," Preval said in a recent interview with Reuters.

On the opposition to his government, he said: "In any election each person wants to win. This happens in every country. This difference doesn't hurt the state as long as the tension doesn't create disorder and the elections are honest."

Preval took power in February last year, succeeding Aristide, the champion of Haiti's poor and oppressed who was ousted by a military coup in 1991 and then restored to power with U.S. intervention in 1994.
Aristide was unable under Haitian law to run for a second consecutive term as president in 1996 but was believed to harbour hopes of running again in the next presidential race.

The government plans a programme of economic reform, including privatisation of state services, which are backed by international donors but are unpopular with many Haitians, most of whom live lives of unrelenting poverty and misery.
On the dock of the Cite Soleil shantytown this week, a 50-year-old woman named Therese tried to sell fish from a tin bowl. She said she had no interest in Sunday's election.
"I don't know about politics. I sell fish, I sell crabs, I believe in God only. I used to believe this government would help but nothing changes, nothing changes," she said.
Therese said she had an extended family of 30 people to look after. If she was lucky she could earn 20 gourds ($1.30) a day selling the fish.
A report by the U.S. International Republican Institute, which is monitoring the poll, said security and authority in many parts of the country were badly lacking.
"This is a serious and long term problem affecting not only the upcoming elections but also Haiti's overall progress toward a more stable democratic society," it said.
It also questioned the impartiality of the Provisional Electoral Council and the job it had done in educating and encouraging voters.

The CEP's Jean Reynold Jean-Pierre conceded that it could have done more to encourage voters but added: "Most people can't read or write. We are still in transition. We have no tradition of democracy and elections. We have to be patient and have courage."
